To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified 6,660 loci that regulate gene expression and have performed a genome wide association scan for these loci in 400 children.
we have identified 28% of the transcripts in lymphoblastoid cells lines that are highly heritable and have mapped the SNPs that regulate these transcripts.
we have identified 15,084 genes whose expression levels are heritable and have performed a genome wide association analysis to identify SNPs that regulate their expression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic variation that influences gene expression.
understanding the role of genetic polymorphisms in regulating gene expression.
the genetic basis of gene regulation and its role in the pathogenesis of complex disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is the most comprehensive genome wide association study for global gene expression ever published.
the study of gene expression is a valuable tool for the discovery of genetic loci that contribute to disease.
this is a comprehensive and detailed study of genetic effects on global gene expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a large proportion of gene expression is heritable and that the heritability is enriched in pathways of interest in the study of complex diseases.
a large number of transcripts are regulated by common genetic variants and these variants can be used to map the genetic basis for disease susceptibility.
a substantial fraction of human gene expression is heritable and is regulated by SNPs in cis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many genes that are heritable and that are regulated by SNPs.

the genetic architecture of gene expression is complex and that the most highly heritable expression traits are enriched in genes involved in cellular stress responses, DNA repair, RNA processing, cell cycle control, immune responses and programmed cell death.
the heritability of gene expression is much greater than the heritability for disease traits.
